utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we please have appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. Good morning, counsel. My name is Mark Harmon. Appearing today will be Carolyn Edgerton and present is Carmela Javier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, counsel. Today we have Daniela Tasic, Chad Mair, Milos Androvic, Tina Drolec, assisting, and two of our interns Eadaoin O'Brien and Akila, whose last name I always have a hard time pronouncing, which is Radhakrishwan, which I'll get to the reporter the spelling. My name is Gregor Guy-Smith and Novak Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Dr. Donia, I know you know the rules of the trade, but still we have to warn you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else by the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and good morning. Just one very quick administrative matter, just dealing with an exhibit that Mr. Lukic spoke to yesterday, P149. You will recall I had mistakenly designated the wrong B/C/S passage as the highlighted passage. We looked into the matter yesterday and found the highlight passage to be at e-court page 138, and I just wanted to let everyone know that passage continues to e-court page 139 as well, just to put that on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, doctor. I trust you've slept well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yesterday we left having dealt with your comments on an ethnic map of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and just related to that, I would like to go back to further explore the strategic objectives of 12 May 1992. Talking specifically about the first objective, which was the demarcation of the state as separate from the other two national communities, could I ask you this: Are you aware of any specific expressions by RS leaders as to how important this objective was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, in his first exposition of the six strategic goals, highlighted that as a -- the most important and overriding goal.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can I then ask that 65 ter number 2134 be displayed, please. In the English, page 52, line 9 from the top of the page to line 15; and B/C/S page 42, line 9 from the bottom of the page. The transcript records my saying 3421. I indicated, I think, 2134. Now, let's deal with the English first. To page 52, please. Could I see page 52 in the English, please. Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honour, while we get warmed up, so to speak. Thank you. Can we have amplified line 9 from the top of the page. And can we go to B/C/S page 42, line 9 from the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But perhaps in the interests of the time, Dr. Donia, while we have the English version in front of you or in front of us, could I draw your attention to the line which begins -- or the sentence which begins "The first goal is the most important one ..."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is this the passage from Mr. Krajisnik that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the first passage to which I refer, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in the event I haven't asked you already, who was Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik was the President of the Bosnian Serb Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder whether this could be marked as the next exhibit, please. So page 52 of the English and page 42 of the B/C/S. 65 ter 2134.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I'm advised that the B/C/S page is not the appropriate page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. That's correct. If we could go to the proper display page, page 42, e-court page 42 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the correct page?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The exhibit is entered into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P339, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In accordance with the practice prescribed yesterday, as no pages from this large document has been previously admitted, if we could have page 1 admitted in there as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. Yes, that's a standing order, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we go next to 02151.02, which is a transcript of the 42nd session of the RS Assembly held in Pale, 19 July 1994. 65 ter number again 2151.02. This will be an extract of comments given by Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, on the English page, which appears on your right, Dr. Donia, could I direct you, please, to a sentence about halfway through the second paragraph on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If you could scroll up, please, Mr. Registrar, the paragraph on the right-hand side, beginning with "We know ..." You'll see it three lines under the number 56 on the right-hand side of this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before I ask for your comment, we'll wait for the B/C/S to be pulled up. And the B/C/S pages have been extracted. That's page 71.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you attribute any significance to Karadzic's comments as to what their primary strategic aim is here in this passage? And, for the record, the highlight passage goes to the sentence which ends with "... anymore."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is his statement of the first strategic goal, or primary strategic aim, as he calls it here, in more explicit form than he stated it on the 12th of May or that is stated in the published version in the Official Gazette of November 1993 when he says, "Our primary strategic aim is to get rid of the enemies in our house and not to be in the same state with them anymore."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in this sentence, when Karadzic refers to enemies in the house, does he stipulate any enemies in particular?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, based, then, on this and other remarks, have you, Dr. Donia, have formed an opinion as to what achieving this objective means?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It meant the creation of a purely Serb state, devoid of Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I ask that 2151.02 be admitted as an exhibit, and I should note that this is an extract of 65 ter number 2151.01, pages of which are admitted as P00219. And the reason for the slightly different 65 ter number is here we're dealing with -- in terms of the English translation, a CLSS finalized translation, so we highlighted the pages on which the highlighted excerpt is contained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And must, then, this be admitted as a separate exhibit or must it go with 219?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think because we've extracted it out - my opinion, subject to what Your Honours think - because we've extracted it out and provided a revised translation of the highlighted pages, it would be best to cross-reference it, rather than make it part of P219.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's admitted as Exhibit P340.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can proceed, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Could I take us next to 65 ter 6703. 6703.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see a document? At this moment we have only the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the English version I don't recognise at all as 6703. Perhaps we can deal with the B/C/S version for the moment until the English version is -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see the documents in B/C/S and English on the screen in front of you, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise what these documents are?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are the B/C/S and English versions respectively of minutes of a meeting held in the office of Croatian President Franjo Tudjman with Nikola Koljevic, then a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and Franjo Boras, a Croat representative, on 8 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The document I see in front of me reads as a date 8 January --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 8 January 1992. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the topics recorded in these minutes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have a view relating to the thing we've just been discussing, the first strategic objective as to the significance of some of the topics discussed at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the meeting Koljevic initiates a discussion about possible population transfers in order to achieve the first strategic goal as it was expressed earlier and approaches the representatives of the Republic of Croatia about the feasibility of working together to achieve ethnic separation and separate states.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you attribute any significance to the fact that this meeting took place some four months before the announcement of the strategic objectives in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This would be one of many expressions by Bosnian Serb leaders well in advance of May 1992 of the general concepts that were inherent in the strategic goals and the first strategic goal in particular, the notion of separation and population transfers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did Nikola Koljevic hold any formal position in the structures of the Bosnian Serb republic, of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at this time because it did not exist yet. But he was subsequently a member of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and after that a vice-president of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could this be marked, please, as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's so marked. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P341, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to go next, please, to 2144.01, transcripts of the 34th session of the RS Assembly held in Jahorina on 30 September 1993, one page of which has previously been marked as P200. Thank you. I see the B/C/S version in front of me. In that regard, I'd like to direct us in the B/C/S to page 230, and in the English translation, page 212 to extract -- an extract from a comment by Velibor Ostojic. So English page 212; B/C/S page 230.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, I know you explained this yesterday, but perhaps you could remind us who Velibor Ostojic was.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time Mr. Ostojic was the Minister of Information of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: English page 212. Thank you. Yes, I think we have the display appropriate on the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I direct you, please, to the very last paragraph where you see Mr. Ostojic speaking on page 212, the second and third line from the bottom of the page, which begins with the sentence "We were aiming to achieve our goal ..."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you attribute any significance to this comment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ostojic is referring to a single goal which very probably is the first or primary strategic goal which we've been speaking and, by content, is identical, which was the ethnical geographic continuity of the Serb population, and of course that would mean -- refer to the notion that all Serbs should be connected somehow geographically, which would also mean the movement of non-Serbs from that territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In this same document, could we please move over to page 33 of the English translation and page 32 of the B/C/S. Your indulgence for just a moment, Your Honours. Now, I'd like to direct us to the last sentence on the bottom of page 33 and -- of the English, that begins with the words "Alija is offering ..." Thank you. And then on the English, if you could go over to page 34, the next page, at the very top of page 34 after this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, this is an excerpt from comments by one Dobrislav Milinkovic. Are you familiar with that name?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a delegate to the Bosnian Serb Assembly. Further, I couldn't identify him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we go over to page 34, please, the very top of the page. Thank you. The end of the highlighted paragraph that began on page 33 with "Alija is offering ..." now appears at the top of page 34, ending with "... there has to be relocation." About four lines down from the top. On the English, could you please scroll back up to the top of the page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to see those comments now, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are they consistent with your view of what the first objective meant?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They are consistent and amount to a reaffirmation of the first strategic goal in the specific circumstances of that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point I wonder if I could ask that these two pages -- no, actually, it would be four pages, pages 212 -- sorry, let me deal with the ones that are in front of me on the screen now. Pages 33 and 34 of the English and page 32 of the B/C/S, and then with respect to the first excerpt, that's page 212 of the English and page 230 of the B/C/S, if they could be admitted as exhibits as part of P200. P200 is this larger document, but only one page has been previously exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Those pages are admitted into evidence as part of Exhibit P200.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And before my friend, Madam Registrar, stands up, I have a note here that the first page of P200 was never previously exhibited.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, page 1 and relevant pages discussed today will be added to the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, given, Dr. Donia, the mix of ethnic communities on the territory of the former Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that we've already spoken about, given the observations that we've made about the meaning behind and importance of the first strategic objective, I'd like to ask you this: Do you have an opinion as to whether these strategic objectives could have been achieved without the use of force?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If he's testifying as a historian, then I believe this is outside of his expertise whether or not -- that particular issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: As an expert witness, Your Honour, he's perfectly entitled to express an opinion based on the breadth of his research, which is exactly what I'm asking him to do here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The objection is that you are asking for an opinion which is outside his area of expertise. That's the nub of the objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In my submission, Your Honour, we have ample evidence before us that he's well-versed in and has conducted an extremely large amount of detailed research into the statements of various Bosnian Serb Assembly delegates, leaders at the Bosnian Serb Assembly sessions, reviewed a breadth of documents, and has conducted detailed researches into demographic changes in the population Bosnia-Herzegovina in the period leading up to and after the war. I fail to see how this would be outside his area of expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'll allow the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion, it would have been impossible to achieve these objectives without the use of force or the immediate and credible threat of force, in other words, at the point of a gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we have this exhibit enlarged, please? I'd like to read something from it. The English version. No, no, no, I'm not suggesting you remove the -- Do you hold that view, Dr. Donia, notwithstanding the fact that the speaker here on this document says that: "Gentlemen, there is no Serbian state in Bosnia in part without gradual depopulation and relocating. If you want ethnically pure Serbian state, and we do, don't we, if we all know and emphasise --" Could we please have it enlarged? Thank you. Thank you so much. "If we all know and emphasise that we cannot live with them, then we have to realise that these draft maps are offering exactly that, and there has to be relocation. This plan has to be accepted and signed by all three sides in order to get three republics. Let us pray to God that other sides accept. And we should chase the devil and accept the offer from God." It comes from the previous page where Alija is allegedly offering something. Now, this seems to me to be a basis for a negotiated settlement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would agree that it -- in the perception of the speaker, Mr. Milinkovic, it was an objective that could be obtained by negotiation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And if the people were prepared to take that perception, then they could sign and do it by negotiated settlement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But I think that the problem was the people which he claimed to speak for proved themselves to be quite unmoved by the prospect of relocating voluntarily in response to some diplomatic agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But then it doesn't seem to me as if that violence was the only alternative here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think from the point of view of those people who were on the ground living in these communities, as I say, it was -- or the immediate and credible threat of violence would be required to achieve that end. And I base that on seeing so many situations or observing, as a historian from a distance, so many situations in the war, in the course of the war, in which territory changed hands and people wanted to stay in their homes. They were not eager to relocate until they saw the point of the gun directed at them. The leaders had a very different notion that this would somehow be a very easy, acceptable process, if only the leaders of the three groups could come together on a solution. The response on the ground was very different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Doctor, do I understand you to be saying that you come to this conclusion based on your observation of other situations elsewhere or based on what you observed happening within Bosnia and Herzegovina amongst the three ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Based on what I observed as a historian among the ethnic groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. And I'm just suggesting that amongst these groups, there is this viewpoint that is expressed by this person here and I'm asking, are you holding to the view that that situation could not be resolved but through violence or the threat of it, notwithstanding this viewpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Prosecutor, I am advised that you are left with about 15 minutes of your time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. I'll endeavour to move forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: As efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, this statement by Mr. Milinkovic made at the 34th session of the RS Assembly was made in September 1993. Are you aware as to whether ethnic cleansing on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina had taken place by that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it had.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you, Dr. Donia, seen any evidence of expressions in the course of your research, expressions by Bosnian Serb leaders that they contemplated the use of force in achieving their territorial objectives?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask, then, that 65 ter number 9150 be displayed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We have a B/C/S document on the screen in front of us. Do you recognise that document, Dr. Donia? And I see the English is now displayed.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a transcript in B/C/S and English respectively of a telephone conversation between Dr. Karadzic and his long-time friend and fellow writer Gojko Djogo on the 12th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you attach any significance to this conversation in terms of the question I've just asked you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is demonstrably a very forceful statement of Karadzic's -- of his contemplation of physical violence and preparedness to use it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In that regard, could we go over, please, to page 3 of the translation and page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you refer to the contemplation of physical violence, looking at the statements at the top of the right-hand -- top of the English-language document on the right-hand side, is this what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask that the transcript of this conversation, Your Honours, be marked as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The exhibit is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P342, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence now for one brief moment, Your Honours. Your Honour, just having a look at the rest of the material, I'd like to go through, I think to be as effective as possible, I would take until the end of this session in my examination-in-chief, and while recognising that this does go over our original estimate, I note that we may, in the event we have saved time with the examination-in-chief of other witnesses, we may transfer that time as the examining party to witnesses. And I'd ask your leave, Your Honour, given that we have saved time in the witnesses up to this date, to just be allowed to go over to the end of this first session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where did you save time, by the way?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't stand corrected, Your Honour. I can't answer your question as directly as I would hope because I need to -- I would need to double-check on which witnesses we have managed to save some time, so my apologies in that regard, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are forgiven.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At what level, in 1992 particularly, Dr. Donia, did ethnic cleansing take place?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ethnic cleansing in the spring and early summer of 1992 really took place at the municipal level. It took place one municipality at a time on different dates over a period of about six, seven weeks, and was executed by local SDS operatives in conjunction with local units of the JNA or paramilitary groups or police forces. So it was very much a municipality-based activity in the spring and early summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've noted that the JNA had a role in that activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in that regard could I direct you to 2065, please. 2065. Page 159 of the English transcript and page 75 of the B/C/S original.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And while we have, albeit sideways, a cover of a document in Serbo-Croatian on the screen, I'd like to ask you: Do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's the cover of a book, a memoire volume by General Veljko Kadijevic, "Moje vidjenje raspada," or "My View of the Breakup."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who was General Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he was the Chief of Staff of the Yugoslav People's Army at that time, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now could I direct you to the passage half way through this page, the middle main paragraph that begins with the sentence "Since the JNA ..." and ends with the words "... never closing the door to cooperation with others." Have you seen that passage?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't see the passage.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On the right-hand side, the large paragraph in the middle of the screen in front of you begins with the sentence "Since the JNA ..."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Does that document support your view that the JNA was involved?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we move one page over now to page 160 of the English translation and page 76 of the original. Just the next page on the English. Just the next page, page 160, of the English. Are you not finding the next page?

utterances.speaker: THE USHER
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If it's not found --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I direct you, Dr. Donia, to the third sentence in this top paragraph that reads "The commands and units of the JNA ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If it could be centralised, please. Could we centralise that page, please, so that we can read the rest of the page. No, to the left. Move it to the left, please. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. And the highlight -- the end of the highlight paragraph ends with "... which would reflect its national interests and goals." Dr. Donia, is this further support of your position?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask these pages be marked as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They are so marked. May they please be given exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P343, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Donia, have you seen evidence during the course of your research that the VJ, the Yugoslav Army, had a role in supporting the VRS in their operations during the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to clarify, the VJ didn't exist at that time. We're talking about the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army. And with that proviso --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Dr. Donia, my question took us forward in time, and my question was: Have you seen evidence during the course of your research that the VJ had a role in supporting the VRS --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- in the operations during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pardon me, I misunderstood the context of your question. Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I take us, please, to 65 ter 00532. 00532.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We seem to be having a difficulty with Mr. Perisic seeing the B/C/S screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is very small, as it appears here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's been consistent for him all day. He hasn't been able to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we suggest that -- thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. We'll make sure that ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we go to page 51 of the English -- of the English, page 51. And, Your Honour, I am -- I may at the end of the session be asking for a brief period of your indulgence in the next session because of these technical things, but, as I said, I am trying to move forward as efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's deal with that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And page 42 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this is an excerpt from the transcript of the tape-recording of the 50th session of the RS Assembly, dated 15 April 1995, a report given by General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I -- your indulgence for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I direct your attention, Dr. Donia, to the paragraph that begins with the words "As an illustration ..." and concludes with "... this year's requirements."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can I have your comment, if any, on this report by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic here is providing very specific information about the source of materiel, weapons, and ammunition from various sources, including from the VJ, and he makes clear that the VJ was a major provider of those provisions in the course of the war up to that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Up to that point being spring 1995, then?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. April 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we move in this same document to page 191, which is an extract from a comment by General Manojlo Milovanovic. English page 191, and B/C/S page 163.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And could we enlarge the B/C/S sufficiently for Mr. Perisic to see.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: English page 191, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your 15 minutes are up, ma'am. Are you ready now with where you saved time?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honour. No, I'm not ready, but people are working to gather the information as to where we saved time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what do we do if we don't find it, and in the meantime you have gone beyond your 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would be asking the Court's indulgence, Your Honour, given the technical and administrative matters that are implied in presentation of testimony that involves such large documents to bear with me for a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You mean you haven't taken them into account when you gave the estimate of the amount of time that you would need for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps I may have been optimistic, Your Honour, to be perfectly honest. I had some familiarity with the import, but I was optimistic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for your honesty. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I'm just not sure, if I can recover myself for a moment, that we have the pages that we're looking for. Page 191 of 532. Thank you. That should be the fourth paragraph on the page. That would be the large paragraph I'd like to direct everyone's attention to, the eighth to eleventh line from the top of the paragraph, and on the B/C/S transcript it's page 163, first paragraph, fifth to ninth line, as I indicated, an extract from a comment by General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: First of all, Dr. Donia, are you familiar with who General Milovanovic is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only that he was a high-ranking general in the VRS by virtue of the fact that only high-ranking generals spoke to the Bosnian Serb Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if I can direct you down to about the seventh line, General Milovanovic begins a comment regarding salaries.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And notes in particular --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, I think we're having some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We've got two counsel standing on the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We have difficulties with the B/C/S page. If you would just read it in English, it could be translated, and then you can figure out what the appropriate page would be at a later point in time. But that way Mr. Perisic would at least be in a position to hear what's being said and would be aware of the particular information that's being discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for the record, I'll indicate again, it will be page 163 of the B/C/S, first paragraph. I'm sorry now I can't read the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was just going to say I hadn't caught up with you where you were talking about salaries on the English, so if you can also sort of show us where.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Seventh line down from the top of this large paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Starting with "Consequently ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Starting with "We did not regard these salaries as charity, nor did we accept them, as somebody from the benches is shouting, in order to serve them ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'm fine. Attend to the B/C/S for Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll continue reading, then, as my friend's requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "We received them following an agreement which the RS Presidency made with the Presidency of Yugoslavia. We never accused you, or rather the state, Why don't you pay us? We know that with your signatures, you made sure that we should be paid by Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, in relation to this theme of support, do you attribute any significance to this comment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It specifically demonstrates the payment of salaries from the Yugoslav government, the Government of Yugoslavia, to officers of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then dealing with these lines from document 00532, or these pages, I'd like to tender them, please, as a Prosecution exhibit and note that already some pages of 532 have been admitted as P312. So my submission, Your Honour, would be that page -- pages 51 and 191 of the English and pages 42 and 163 of the B/C/S be admitted as the -- as Prosecution exhibits, part of P312, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They are so admitted, and they will form part of Exhibit P312.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The pages are added, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And could we turn, please, to 2160.01, parts of which are admitted, as far as I understand - and I'll double-check with Ms. Javier - as P231.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is correct. And what pages of that 65 ter number do you now want?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, please, Your Honour. Page 73 of the English and page 93 of the B/C/S. Would you please scroll down to the third paragraph. No, I'm sorry, that's not the correct page, and my apologies, Your Honour. Your indulgence for a moment. I'll move on, Your Honour, rather than take some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you want to do with this 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I want to scroll up. I've actually just spotted the sentence that I was looking for. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Halfway through this first paragraph, which is an extract of a passage from General -- from Dr. Karadzic during the 53rd session of the RS Assembly held in Jahorina on 28 August 1995. I'd like to direct everyone to the line that begins halfway through this first paragraph "Gentlemen, one should know that we took over personnel ..." Do you see that, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's within this sentence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sentence actually begins "You know that well ..." and then on the following line, continues, "Gentlemen, one should know that we took over personnel." Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Down to the sentence that ends with "... we were also given a large amount."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is this articulation by Dr. Karadzic consistent with your position?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, could I ask that this page be admitted, please, as the next Prosecution Exhibit? That's page 73 and B/C/S page 93. I should note some pages have been exhibited, as I said earlier, as part of P231. Could they be added to P231.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This page is so admitted, and it is added to Exhibit P231.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The page is added, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have the basic data that we were looking for. We'd like to compute this at the break and then report back in detail to you after the break, if that could be possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to one final area now please, Dr. Donia, and that's related to the fifth strategic objective, partition of the city of Sarajevo into Serbian and Muslim sections and the establishment of an effective state authority in each section. Do you have a view based on your detailed research into Sarajevo and related to your report on the background of the siege of Sarajevo as to the rationale behind the siege of the city?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Bosnian Serb leaders viewed the siege of Sarajevo as necessary to prevent the functioning of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and as a critical collective hostage, creating in Sarajevo a collective hostage which would be of value in gaining concessions from the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and from the international community.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I turn to 65 ter 2301.01, which is an excerpt from a transcript of the 17th session of the RS Assembly, held in Jahorina in July 1992. English page 15; B/C/S page 13. Do you recognise the -- thank you. I'd like to draw everyone's attention to an excerpt from a comment by Radovan Karadzic in the English page at line 8 and B/C/S page 13, lines approximately 17, 18, and 19.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, do you see the sentence that begins with the word "Thanks to the Sarajevo battlefield ..."?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Ending with "... was never established outside Yugoslavia." Is this consistent with your position?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could this page, please, be marked as the next Prosecution exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted into evidence. May it be so marked, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, pages 1, page 13 in the English and page 13 in B/C/S will become Exhibit number P344.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you comment or describe for the Trial Chamber the geographical situation of the city of Sarajevo, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The city grew up in a narrow valley, east-west valley that is narrowest at its east point and widens as one goes to the west in the city to become actually a plain, the Sarajevo plain, to the west. Consequently the historic centre of the city is surrounded by -- flanked on at both north and south by relatively high hills which render the valley position very visible and vulnerable to anyone who would come in and wish to subdue the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in your report prepared for the Dragomir Milosevic case, you talk about the political and military surrounding of the city of Sarajevo, but I wonder if you're in a position to relate this to the fifth objective, partition of the city of Sarajevo? Do you see any congruity between the surrounding of the city and the partition of the city?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that congruence lies in the demographic distribution within the city itself and in its surrounding hills, or perhaps more accurately, the Bosnian Serb leaders' understanding of the demographic distribution. Specifically, the city itself, the urban part located in that valley, that east-west valley, was very ethnically mixed and at many points in the highrise communities, ethnically indeterminate or completely mixed by individual apartment. The surrounding hills had historically, that is, say, from the nineteenth century, been largely inhabited by Serb -- by Serb peasants and rural villages. That was diluted somewhat in the course of the latter part of the twentieth century, but nonetheless the distinction can still be seen in the census numbers from 1991. Therefore, the concept of division really amounted to encirclement in this situation based on the Serb notion, the notion of the Bosnian Serb nationalist leaders that the surrounding areas would be Serbian and the centre of the city would be what they call its Muslim part.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you seen evidence in your research that would reflect how important the Sarajevo battlefield was to Bosnian Serb leaders?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: One final exhibit, then. 65 ter 2301.01, please. English page 15; B/C/S page 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We have just had that as Exhibit P344, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we please go back to P344, then. Thank you, Your Honours. There's a further passage I'd like Dr. Donia to highlight. After that, Your Honours, one or two very short areas, and I note the time that I estimate wouldn't be longer than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We're at the time for break actually right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can't add two more points, but go back to P344, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Alternatively, Your Honour, if we -- with respect, if we take the break now, I might be able to profit from a few minutes to deliver the figures that I had promised to Your Honour accurately and make sure the technical side of this goes smoothly so we can conclude with some measure of alacrity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We'll then take a break and come back at a quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I may, I'd like to report back to you on the matter of where we had gained time, Your Honour, from our estimates. Shall I do that? Although it won't be a complete picture, you can appreciate it's a complicated calculation that Ms. Javier has been doing exclusively, but I'd like to advise you and report back, as I indicated, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In respect of the evidence of Mr. van Lynden, it was estimated 3 hours, and the Prosecution took 2 hours and 27 minutes, approximately, so a gain of approximately 30 minutes. In respect of the estimated time for the witness MP-229, the estimated time for examination-in-chief was 30 minutes and the Prosecution took approximately 15 minutes, so there a further gain. In respect of the witness Slavica Livnjak, the estimated time was 1 hour; the time for examination-in-chief, 30 minutes, so again an approximate gain of 30 minutes. Would you like me to go on, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've just been doing calculations. So far you've got 45 minutes saved, which taken the time you've taken with this witness, you have a credit of 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope I'll only need to ask for your indulgence for a credit of about half of that, 20 minutes or so, to conclude, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Having looked at P334, the passage I would have highlighted is incorporated into the exhibit. So I'd like to move to two more final exhibits, but let me ask this question of the witness first.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, we left talking about -- we left where, at page 28, lines 15 to 18, you equated the concept of division to encirclement with regard to the situation in Sarajevo, and I'd like to ask you this: Can you date -- or have you seen any evidence of Bosnian Serb leaders contemplating encirclement of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recall where that might have been?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 16th Assembly session discussed encirclement. It was referenced in a number of other -- Bosnian Serb nationalist leaders referenced the concept of encirclement in a number of other Assembly sessions as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps I could ask that 65 ter 9148 be displayed, which is a transcript of an intercepted telephone conversation between Radovan Karadzic and Slobodan Milosevic on September 9, 1991. It appears in B/C/S on the left.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this transcripted conversation, Dr. Donia, which now appears in B/C/S -- or in English on the left?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I could take us to page 4 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S, the very last paragraph in respect of both of those versions. Can we at all have the -- all right. We have B/C/S on the left. Can we have the English on the right? Wonderful, thank you. Can I direct you to Radovan Karadzic's comment at the very bottom of the page, please, on the English, very bottom of the page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Where Karadzic says: "Let them do this as soon as possible ..." to Slobodan Milosevic. I'd like to ask you two questions. How do you interpret Karadzic's comment in this conversation? No, actually, first, could I just ask you to, in a nutshell, explain to the Trial Chamber the context within which this conversation takes place.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The conversation took place in the midst of a situation along the border between Bosnia-Herzegovina on the one hand and Croatia on the other in which Milan Martic, the designated Minister of the Interior of the Serb entity in Krajina had been detained by police of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the tiny town of Otok, and this had angered Karadzic to the point where he was calling for the -- he was asking Milosevic to get the JNA to intervene to liberate Martic from the custody of the Bosnian police. This touched off a number of conversations between Karadzic, Milosevic, and several other leaders of the Bosnian Serbs, in an effort to make this happen. And in the course of this particular conversation, Karadzic is reporting that he has received word that the people from the area of Romanija were preparing to cut off access to the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you attribute any significance to this comment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is the first time that I've seen -- chronologically it's the first time that I note Karadzic expressing the possibility of isolating, cutting off, Sarajevo as an act of, in a sense, revenge or retaliation against something that the Bosnian Muslim leaders were doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask that this transcript 9148 be tendered as a Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted as an exhibit. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P345, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the final exhibit, 65 ter 9149, being a transcript of an intercepted conversation, the same date, between Radovan Karadzic and Nikola Koljevic. 9149. I see the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, I'd like to ask you, is this one of the string of conversations you -- or a number of conversations you were referring to at page 33, line 11, just now?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we move in both documents over to page 2, please. Could I just direct everyone in the English version to the seventh line from the top where Karadzic is noted as the speaker and he -- can you scroll up, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And he says, "They'll cut off Sarajevo ..."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have any comment or attribute any significance to this conversation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is very similar to the statement that he made to Milosevic in approximately the same time frame and refers to the isolation or cutting off of Sarajevo as a possible course of action.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If this is the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P346, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And a final area, please, Dr. Donia. I'd like to know, given your experience in events in the city of Sarajevo, in particular over the years, have you seen public evidence that the citizens of Sarajevo were targeted by -- or were the subject of shelling and sniping during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: A couple of things. First of all, this is certainly outside the proffered area of his testimony, that being an expert historian, and he is now -- is he now being offered as a fact witness? I mean, if so, so be it, and I'll deal with it as you will. But I'm somewhat taken aback.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton, do you have any response?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. If I can just have a moment to turn to the page of Dr. Donia's report. Actually, it's a series of pages, and without having the e-court number, there's a chapter in his report called "Sarajevo and its Siege in the International Spotlight," and on the actual document it's pages 29, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34, and part of page 35, that touch on the subject of public exposure of events in the city of Sarajevo during the course of the siege, and the question was merely relating to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You say that's from page?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of the document, page 29. In fact, that whole chapter, Your Honour, generally deals with the international reaction to the events in Sarajevo, and related to that theme, I'm simply asking him about public evidence, and depending on the witness's answer, I may go further with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is this the chapter that's headed "International Diplomacy"?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. It's headed "Sarajevo and its Siege in the International Spotlight."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: On reflection, I'll let it go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may just have a moment to go back to my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Dr. Donia, have you seen evidence during the course of your research that the citizens of Sarajevo were the subject of -- public evidence that the citizens of Sarajevo were the subject of shelling and sniping during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And is that evidence in the media?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- there was a great deal of evidence that was disseminated by international media and regional media about shelling and sniping directed against the city of Sarajevo or civilians in the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you say "regional media," can you identify any media sources in particular?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the media sources are numerous. Certainly the media within Sarajevo. Sarajevo Television and Oslobodjenje carried reports of this, as well as publications like The New York Times, Christian Science Monitor, Washington Post, and, on occasion, media based in Belgrade or Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you recall, and if you don't, please indicate, but do you recall which media sources based in Belgrade -- or any media sources based in Belgrade or Zagreb in particular?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the wire service TANJUG carried very pointed, very excellent coverage of the siege and the general situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina throughout the war, and that was often picked up by other publications, print publications. And visual media in Belgrade as well did from time to time. I recall seeing such reports, but I don't remember the specific origin of the footage that was carried.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just one last question to round things off. Could you explain what TANJUG was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: TANJUG was the -- originated in the Yugoslav socialist era. It was the official wire-service provider for newspapers throughout the former Yugoslavia, equivalent of AP and/or the French Press Agency.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with that answer, that concludes my examination-in-chief. Of course, at the end of his testimony altogether, I'll have a motion with respect to his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton, before you sit down, yesterday you referred to a couple of 65 ter documents, and when I asked you what you intended to do with them, you said I'm still using them. I'll deal with them at the end, an nothing ended up happening to those documents. That was 65 ter 02619, 02290, and 09224. What do you want to do with those 65 ter documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I recognise the first two numbers you gave me as the 65 ter numbers of the reports upon which Dr. Donia has based his testimony, and at the beginning of his testimony, I indicated that the way I interpreted the Chamber's guidance in their decision as to Dr. Donia's reports overall was that the Chamber would be prepared to consider the admission of those reports at the conclusion of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. So 02619 and 02290 are Dr. Donia's reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good. Now, 09224?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That was -- oh, and if I may, Your Honour, you've just mentioned 2619, but the 65 ter is 2169, I'm advised. Oh, I don't know. I think Ms. Javier is going on my list of those numbers, and before I correct anybody, I should double-check what exactly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think you should.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. You've seen I have this tendency now. 9224, Your Honour, is the map. I'll just check which one it was. But there was a map which Dr. Donia used to illustrate ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Edgerton. Madam Registrar has helped us. That was the census map, and it was admitted as Exhibit P338.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that was his marked map which was admitted as P338, and I'm wondering if it would assist everyone, for our record-keeping, if I asked now for the unmarked map to be tendered as well. If it's useful, I think, for everyone in reviewing things later on to have a map that's unmarked with nothing obscured with the marks the witness might have made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the 65 ter number of the unmarked map?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 9224, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But 9224 is now the marked map.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's the whole question of technology, and some of us are completely illiterate in that field.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You're not alone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then the registrar says that 09224 will also be admitted as the clean map, the unmarked map, and at the same time as the marked map. Don't ask me how that happens. The registrar can help us. Yes, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P347, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. All I say, and I still say this with my admission that I don't understand technology, we now have two 09224 65 ter numbers, being Exhibit P338 and Exhibit P347. This is what we are trying to avoid all this time. Now we're creating it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, ma'am. You have finished your cross-examination, you said?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, that concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's all right, Your Honour. That's fine. Thank you very much, and thank you for your patience. Thank you, Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fifteen seconds, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just so I want to make sure that we start off on the right foot, do you prefer to be called Dr. Donia or Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You may call me Mr. Donia or anything you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You can call me Ray, you can call me Jay, one of those.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to start for a moment, if I could, to see if I can get an understanding of your background, and by that I'm specifically referring to your background with regard to your studies in history and what you've done in your life, if I may.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as I understand the review of your CV, you, I believe, went to the University of Michigan where you studied history.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my graduate studies, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And there you became enamoured with, and I use the word in a positive sense, you became enamoured with a particular region of the world and a particular people.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My first encounter and becoming enamoured with the former Yugoslavia was in 1965 when I was an undergraduate at Hope College, and then I renewed that in graduate school in Michigan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. In that regard, I think it would be fair to say that you've travelled a long road in terms of attempting to understand many of the disparate views and disparate issues that revolved around, for the moment what I'll call, the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you spent some time, and I don't want to go way back in history because, among other things, I don't think we really have the time, but apart from that, I don't know how fruitful it will ultimately be, but you spent a fair amount of time dealing with the history of those peoples, and I'm using that as a collective sense for the moment, before the twentieth century.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There came a time when you left college and you went into the world of business.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I left -- went into the world of business to work for Merrill Lynch in 1981 when I was -- at that time I'd been teaching at the University of Oregon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you left to move into the world of business, that occurred at a point in time when the economy of the United States was slightly different than it is today.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was closer to the same, unfortunately, at that time. It was not good.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It got better.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It got better.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And better and better, if you were, for example, in the market, and by that I'm referring to the stock market.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it got better in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, you profited handsomely from your work, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as a result of what you were able to do in that regard, you, as a matter of fact, if I'm not mistaken, have endowed the University of Michigan with a charitable trust of about two and a half million dollars; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Altogether that's the sum, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that endowment is an endowment for the purposes of studying various aspects of history; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is an endowment for a professorship, the Fred Cuny professorship, a university professorship, in the history of human rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Apart from that, I take a slight digression for a moment. I know that you've testified on a number of occasions here, and I believe that this is a question that you've been asked a number of times. I ask you that same question which deals with what I believe to be the Donja Vakuf foundation, which is a foundation that you started; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that's a foundation that focuses itself on any particular issue, or is that a foundation, once again, a generalised foundation that gives -- that gives funds to those people that are deemed to be deserving within the context of historical studies?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, let me say it doesn't exist anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I closed it three years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The board of directors closed it three years ago with a terminal donation to the University of Michigan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So what happened is those funds -- the Donja Vakuf funds transferred over into the charitable trust that I mentioned a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Directly to the endowment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. While the Donja Vakuf Foundation was in existence, who were the individuals who made a determination as to how those funds, if funds were to be dispersed to anyone?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our family. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's fine. I need no more than that. And did you at that -- during the period of time that the foundation was in existence, did you make a determination to fund individuals in Bosnia who were involved in historical research or human rights work?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT REPORTER
utterances.text: Is there another mic to your right that you could use instead? I'm just picking up --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm happy to do whatever you want me to do, and if my voice is dropping, I told her to yell at me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your neighbour was fidgeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I also told her to yell at me whenever she couldn't hear me. Is that better?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT REPORTER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned in your testimony earlier, I believe --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I tell all parties right now that we are struggling a little bit with regard to the issue of reference pages for yesterday. The printers in the Defence room, one is out of ink; the other one is not working. We have the -- the daily from yesterday which we have been operating off of. We have attempted to transpose the numbers over to the daily that I was using yesterday. So if I misstate a page at any point in time, if you need a page reference, I apologise. But we're trying to get an appropriate official transcript printed; however, there are X number of teams working, and it's an administrative issue. Hopefully, I don't think we are going to run into too many problems. Just so you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned, I believe, yesterday that you were going to be teaching this summer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll be teaching this winter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This winter.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Starting in January.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And is that at the University of Michigan?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's the university that you've endowed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You're going to be teaching history of some fashion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'll be teaching -- I will be teaching and coordinating a survey course in the study of Eastern Europe, interdisciplinary course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is that a course that you teach as a full professor, as an associate professor, as a visiting professor?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a visiting professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. Now, again, you indicated that you have been appointed to the academy, if I'm not mistaken, and I want to make sure I've got this term correct, The Academy of Sciences in Bosnia-Herzegovina, somewhat recently, as a member.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a corresponding member.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Corresponding member, thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that particular academy, that's for Islamic studies, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What is that academy for?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Academy of Arts and Sciences of Bosnia-Herzegovina is a academic consortium which admits members or regularly recognises people by membership for their scholarly achievements. It's been there since -- it's been there about 55 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And at this point in time, there are a fair number of -- there are a fair number of Serbian members, are there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I don't know. I actually was going to look. Certainly, the majority of members are not Serbs or Croats, but there are some Serbs and some Croats who are members of the Academy of Arts and Sciences.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And do you think that the majority being such fall into some of the same theoretical bases that you've suggested to us here, which is that the decision as to who is going to be in that particular academy is a constructed one, as opposed to a primordial one? In this sense, what I'm trying to suggest to you is that if it was a primordial one, then the issue would be one of, as a term you've used, intellectual merit, and if it was a primordial one, then it would be one that would be, let's say, a group identifiable, and in this particular situation a group identifiable of individuals as being neither Croat or Serb, as you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. You are not -- just so we're clear, because you know a number of times I've stood and objecting with regard to the area of your expertise, so I'd like to make sure we've defined the area of your expertise. You are not a political scientist.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You are not an anthropologist?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sociologist?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Psychologist?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Psychiatrist?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very much not so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very much not so. A demographer?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Statistician?
