utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Political scientist.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the second time I'm not, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I apologise; I don't think I said that. So I did. Lawyer?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Anthropologist I've mentioned. Archaeologist, obviously, you're not, because that would be a harder science.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe that I've covered the social sciences generally, have I not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say geography, if you wish. I'm not a geographer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. And once again, just in terms of dealing with your expertise, you are not a linguist?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you learned what I will call B/C/S late in life; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And without asking your age, because as my constitutional law professor told me the two questions you never ask a woman, one is her age and the other is whether she's a member of the communist party, being an American, I have no interest in your age, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not suggesting the witness is a woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, I'm not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Neither am I a member of the communist party.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: How old were you when you first learned the language?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm 63 years old now, and I started learning B/C/S before it was called B/C/S by anybody at graduate school at the University of Michigan in 1973.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. So you've been working with the language for some 30-plus years.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you've told us that your speaking is good, your reading and your writing, I believe, are both very good, or something like that. I mean they are above adequate, in any event.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said my speaking was very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My reading is very good, and my writing is good.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. In that regard, when you were doing research in the original language, did you do all of the work by yourself? And by that I mean did you read the original documents and then translate them for purposes of your work?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It varied.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are some documents for which -- first of all, there are some documents in English. There are --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With no translation, obviously.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are some documents that I encountered only in B/C/S, typically noted, those documents -- that is, made notes of is documents in English, and then in some cases subsequently translated them myself. In general, I prefer to work with English translations; mine if I have to, other peoples if they are available.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue, first of all, of your translation efforts and those alone, and I understand that you're not in a position to quantify the number of documents that you translated on your own and then used for purposes of your research or your reports, in that regard did you obtain the benefit of anybody who was conversant in the language to a greater degree than you are? And by that I mean it was their mother tongue?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very occasionally. Every once in awhile I would consult someone about a phrase that I couldn't quite understand or didn't make sense to me, but probably in the course of the whole thing, not more than 10, 15 times.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And as you've told us, you preferred to work in English, so to a certain extent what you were doing is you were relying on documents that had been translated by someone else for purposes of your reports and research, the documents initially being in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In almost all cases I either encountered those in B/C/S or had the benefit of seeing them in both languages if the document originated in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. As I understood your testimony, your craft consists of principally writing history. Those were the words that you used.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in that regard you've described, among other things, that you use -- and now I'm referring to the reports that are the subject matter of your discussion here, and that was a report that you prepared, I believe, in 2002, which is presently identified as 20619, 65 ter number, and a report that you prepared in 2006, which is presently identified as 65 ter number 02290. And I'm just doing that for purposes of the record and for nothing more. You've described to us that you used a narrative form in those reports for purposes of conveying the information that you deemed appropriate.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before you wrote the first report, and that's the report in 2002, could you tell us, please -- and that's the report -- do you remember which case you did that report for?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the report for the Krajisnik case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Before you began writing that report, were you supplied with any documents by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What were you supplied with?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was supplied with the transcripts and minutes of a number of sessions, not all but a number of sessions, of what you have suggested we call the Bosnian Serb Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also was provided with some documents from the SDS minutes and correspondence that were left in the SDS -- were acquired by the Office of the Prosecutor from SDS sources in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You were also supplied with a copy of the indictment, were you not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the same would be true in regard to the report that you prepared in 2006. You were supplied with a series of documents; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you were supplied with a copy of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the report that you prepared in 2002, were there any memorialised conversations or communications with regard to the purpose of your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the report in 2006, were there any memorialised conversations or communications with regard to the purpose of that report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard, then, to the first report, the report that you prepared in 2002, who were you dealing with for purposes of this report? And by that I mean who called you or how were you contacted in the first instance for purposes of determining whether or not you were in a position to supply the Prosecution with a report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Alan Tieger contacted me, a prosecutor with the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when Mr. Tieger contacted you, he indicated -- once again, I'm putting this in terms of general subject matter, not in terms of specific words, he indicated that he was involved in a prosecution, was the prosecution of a particular individual, that individual was Mr. Krajisnik, and he wished for you to assist him in preparing a report with regard to information that he was concerned with to further his prosecution, and in that regard he also gave you a copy of the indictment so you would be aware of the facts as he perceived them to be.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aware of the facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The facts, as he perceived them to be.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And aware of the -- without getting involved in the law, aware of the theoretical bases upon which he was intending to proceed with his prosecution.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't say he -- he didn't provide me with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, when you read the indictment, the indictment supplied that to you, did it not? The indictment said more than just fact, fact, fact. It gave you information concerning what the theories were upon which the Prosecution believed there was liability as regards Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar enough with the legal interpretation of this, but he never, nor did the indictment, give me an idea of the theory that he was proceeding on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did the indictment give you an idea of what criminal activity Mr. Tieger believed Mr. Krajisnik was guilty of?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And it identified certain crimes; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Alleged crimes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And it -- very well. And it identified what Mr. Tieger believed Mr. Krajisnik's role was in those crimes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And that was information that you were armed with before you undertook the writing of this report.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the same would be true for the report that you wrote in 2006 with regard to Mr. Milosevic, Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, those are not the only cases that you've been involved in. This is either your ninth or tenth case here.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somewhere around 12 or 13, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I was looking at your CV. I think I got up to -- I got up to nine, but perhaps there are more. In each of those cases, were you supplied with an indictment by the Prosecutor to assist you in an understanding of what they were seeking to prove against particular individuals?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, either supplied with or directed to on a web site.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And as a matter of fact, an examination of the indictment, for your purposes to be fair, is a critical document in understanding the nature and contours and parameters of the report that you were going to write.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the topic of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. Just in passing here, you were asked the question, I believe, of whether or not you've ever testified or been approached by the Defence for purposes of writing a report on behalf of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered that I had -- I never had.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the answer was you had not. Well, considering your expertise, I wish to pose to you just for a moment just a quick hypothetical question, which is based upon your view, if the Defence were to approach you and ask you to submit a report which, for example, the assertion of a defence for purposes of countering the charges against the defendant, for example, a defence that an attempt to legitimise the Bosnian war by arguing that Serbia and Croatia's claims to the area have been long-standing and that Bosnia-Herzegovina was and still is part of a medieval Croatia, would you undertake that task?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm always looking for work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I think the answer to the question is, if I prepare the report that I am prepared to prepare on such a topic, will it be accepted by the person commissioning it as useful, and the answer to that question has normally been yes, but not always.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My question is slightly different, I think, which is: As an expert historian, if you were asked to -- if I called you up on the phone and said, Listen, my client is being charged, and this is the defence, and I believe there is a historical basis to this defence and I would like to have your involved, I'd like for you to write this report for me, sir, because you're the expert, would you undertake that task? For example, the example that I just gave you, which is that the Bosnian war was legitimate and the argument that I wish to pose is that Serbia and Croatia's claims to the area have been long-standing and that Bosnia-Herzegovina was and still is part of medieval Croatia. Would you do it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would do it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You would do it.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, similarly, if I was going to make a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just for my own understanding, when we say the Bosnian war is legitimate, who is speaking? Is this from the perspective of the Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is -- this would be from the standpoint of an individual who is being charged who is either Serbian or Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Not Bosnian, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So by "Bosnian war," you mean that the attack of Bosnia by some outsider.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult -- I think you've focused on one of the issues as kind of difficult. It's hard to really determine who -- and I'm doing this internally here for the moment. There were a number of different factions or sides within what has been called the Bosnian war, so let me be more specific because I think I understand what your concern may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Having the Judge's question in mind, I'm defending a Croatian general. Based upon all of the information that you have, would you undertake the task, as I've framed it here?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure how you've framed it, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, which is -- let me do it again. Which is to legitimise -- my position is that -- as Croatian general is that my activity was legitimate. The war I fought was a legitimate war. And the reason it was legitimate was because the -- my claims to the area have been long-standing and that area, Bosnia-Herzegovina, was and still is part of medieval Croatia. Would you undertake to write that report to me?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that report, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. So if I called you up and said, This is what I want, this is my defence, you would say, Listen, I can't do that, I'm sorry, because based upon my assessment of history, that is not something I can do.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I were to mount -- if I were to mount another potential defence argument that -- well, I won't do that. That's okay. And the reason that you wouldn't do what I suggested is because you have at this point, and you've had for some years, a definite view of who is responsible for criminal behaviour with regard to the Bosnia-Herzegovina conflict between the years of 1990 - I'm starting a little bit before - up to and including the signing of the Dayton Accord, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In all fairness -- you don't?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you've posed that question, no. You've kind of mixed two concepts here of criminal behaviour and the sources of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I think those are different issues. My views on criminal behaviour would have to be further, you know, broken down by particular situations, and those of the conflict in general would be -- may be more germane, more accessible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to the cases that we've discussed in a very general sense in terms of cases you've been asked for assistance by the Prosecution, were you asked to assist the Prosecution with regard to the Delic case, to write a report in Delic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oric?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Or Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Those are all cases that involved Muslim defendants; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You said just a moment ago that your views on criminal behaviour would have to be broken down by particular situations. So I'd like to spend a moment there, if I could. With regard to your views on, for example, Slobodan Milosevic, you have a definite view with regard to his criminal responsibility, do you not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You believe that he's guilty of the crimes for which he was charged, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is a view that you have, as a matter of fact, articulated on more than one occasion.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is a view that you have, as a matter of fact, and we may discuss it later, you've actually sent at least one letter concerning your position about the judgement that was rendered by the International Court of Justice as being a political decision because they didn't use certain information.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I sent a letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You signed a letter that was sent by 54 -- you and 54 of your colleagues; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in that letter you made it very clear that in your estimation, Milosevic was guilty.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you also made it very clear that as far as you were concerned, the judgement finding -- the finding of that court was a political decision that, as a matter of fact, avoided what you believed to be compelling evidence that should have brought them to a different position.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, concerning Milosevic, I want to talk about Milosevic now for a moment not as an individual but as a leader, because one of the terms that you have used I think a fair amount is "Serb leaders" or "Bosnian Serb leaders"; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I have, as a matter of fact, have asked -- and you have been very kind in that regard to identify when you were dealing with Bosnian leaders, as opposed to when you were dealing with Serb leaders.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I normally use the term Bosnian Serb nationalist leaders in reference to the people we were talking about in the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When we're talking about Bosnian Serb nationalist leaders, you're discussing such people as Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And based upon your historical review, am I correct -- not am I correct, but is your view that General Mladic was subordinate to Mr. Karadzic, as the president?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And Mr. Karadzic, he was the -- he was like -- he was like George Bush, the one who's just -- who will be leaving shortly. He was the Commander-in-Chief.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't tempt me, but -- he was the Commander-in-Chief of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I just want to make sure you were on the same page there.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we are, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the -- in terms of the Serb leadership, and now I'm not using the term "Bosnian Serb nationalist leadership" but the Serb leadership, you count among those, I would take it, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And by that I'm talking about Slobodan Milosevic, not the Milosevic in whose case you testified in.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Although you testified in both, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two Milosevics, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You've done two Milosevics. You've done Slobodan and you've done Dragomir.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in the Dragomir Milosevic case is the case involving the 2006 report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is the report before you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He was in a slightly different position. You wouldn't consider him to be Serb leadership, would you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would consider him to be part of the Bosnian Serb leadership on the military side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And for the moment, taking a look at Milosevic, would you consider Lilic -- do you know who he is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would you consider him to be part of the leadership?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the leadership of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, now that we have introduced two Milosevics, may I suggest that each time you refer to a Milosevic, you tell us which one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I shall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You've just said at line 13 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm with you. I'm totally with you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When I said "take a look at Milosevic," I was speaking about Slobodan Milosevic."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to Slobodan Milosevic, he was involved with his group of people involved, for example, Mr. Lilic.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And Mr. Lilic was the president of what, precisely, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he was the President of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As reconstituted in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say "as reconstituted," that's when the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia became the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The FRY, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. We'll talk about that in a bit. Have you -- I want to move away from that for a moment or two and discuss the issue of how you compiled the information that you used for your first report, the report that you submitted in 2002, "The Origins of Republika Srpska, 1990-1992 - A Background Report."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to that report, did you, as you were preparing that report, apart from the documents you discussed with us earlier that you received from the Prosecution, did you ask the Prosecution for an index of a list of the documents that they had available so that you could search through that list and make a determination of what documents they had that were available might be germane to you compiling your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You did not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And as a matter of fact, the same would be true, would it not, of the report that you compiled in 2006, that report which is entitled "From Elections to Stalemate: The Making of the Sarajevo Siege, 1990-1994."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At some point, I think at some point in time in some previous case, you were asked the question of whether or not it would be an important thing to do, so that you had gone through a comprehensive analysis and research of all the information that was available, and I believe you said something to the effect, and I may be paraphrasing, that, No, life is too short to do that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is too short to do that. But at the same time, I ask them to give me whatever they can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My question was slightly different than that, Dr. Donia. When you were asked the question in the previous proceedings, and you said something to the effect, No, that's not something I would do.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly what I said. I would have to see the document to be able to affirmatively answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me see if I can refresh your recollection.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You were asked the following question, and this is the proceedings on Wednesday, 10 May 2006, in the Prlic case, page 1861, case number IT-01-74-T, you were asked the following question and gave the following response, which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you give us the line, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Starting at line 9 through 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "All right. Do you by chance ask for an index so that you would know the documents they might have, because, after all, let me cue you in, the Prosecution has been going around the former Yugoslavia having access to various archives. All right. Did you ask by any chance, Could I look at the list of the documents from the various archives, be they from the BiH, be they from Croatia, and so on and so forth? Did you ever ask for that list?" And your answer is: "No, life is too short to look over that list in one of those archives alone." Does that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That was your position then?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that's your position now?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So the body of information that you're relying upon -- I'm sorry, that you relied upon, because we're now talking about two reports you've done in the past, is that information which, in large measure, was supplied to you by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Do you think, while we're here just at this moment, do you think that it's important for a fact-finder to have available to them from an expert, such as yourself, as comprehensive a report as possible that discusses all sides of the situation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And is that something which you believe with regard to the two reports that we're discussing right now, the one prepared in 2002 and the one that you prepared in 2006, is something that you did, that you prepared as comprehensive a report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the limits of the guidelines that were requested of me by the Prosecution at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. You've -- within the limits of the guidelines.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the issue of preparing as comprehensive a report as possible, you've taken a different position in that regard, have you not, in your testimony here before the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. You'll have to suggest a ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me see what I can do here. I'm referring the Court and counsel to 1858, proceedings on 10 May 2006, case number IT-04-74-T, commencing at page -- at line 15, on page 1858. Question: "Okay. Do you think --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said you're referring to? There's a word I don't understand on the screen. When you started that sentence. "I'm referring to ..." something something, "... counsel to 1858."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Got it. I'm with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "Okay. Do you think, do you think, and help me out here, but do you think it would be member for the honourable members of our Trial Chamber to have that information so at least you could say, Well, here's what I looked at, here's what I agree with, here's what I don't agree with, here's what I came up with my conclusion and here's why. Do you think that might be important?" And your answer is: "I think that would be up to the honourable judges to decide. My own purpose is, let's say, more restricted than that. It is to provide a narrative account which can, in fact, be challenged and alternative interpretations presented. But, again, I don't want to run into 200 pages or multiple volumes for the purpose of historical background." I continue, moving to page 1859, line 3: Question: "That wasn't my question. Do you think it would be important for the Trial Chamber to have a comprehensive report from an historian such as yourself, if indeed that is what you are coming here to testify about, historical facts and drawing conclusions?" And your answer: "No." So my question to you is: You've taken a different position with regard to this same issue in a previous proceeding; correct.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see how it's different.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just so that I don't forget, my question wasn't answered. What case is that? Maybe it will answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That case is the Prlic case, and the case number is IT-04-74-T.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Would that be a convenient point in time?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To pick up where we left off, if I could, since your work on these two reports, am I correct in my understanding that you have not edited, modified, them in any substantial regard. I know you've made some corrections. But with regard to the report that has been submitted here, a report that you've done in 2002, that report remains essentially in the same iteration that it was when you initially submitted it; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the report that you did in 2006, that report similarly remains in the same iteration. There have been some, I think, maybe minor modifications, corrections.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Corrections, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You haven't -- you haven't really --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't rewritten it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You haven't worked it over.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard -- with regard to those two reports, because the question I have is the same for both of them, have you had a chance to reflect and make a determination of whether or not any further information should be included in those reports based upon the work that you've done since 2002 or the work you've done since 2006?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I actually did expand substantially the topics that I covered in the 2006 report in my book on Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the answer is yes, I have contemplated and certainly see areas that could be added or expanded through both documentation that's newly available to me and other work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you do that -- you did that expansion in your book, you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not with the reports themselves.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that at the time that you wrote those reports, that your purpose was not to be comprehensive; it was, in fact, to be synthetic, to be a provider of a digested, abbreviated account of these topics.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would say concise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Did you take a different position or, put in other terms, did you take the precise position that I just mentioned to you when testifying in the Prlic case?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Let me see if I can refresh your recollection in that regard, Mr. Donia. I don't believe we need the specific language before us because it's a relatively long question and answer on page 1863. But going on to page 1864, lines 4 through 6: "I would again say my purpose here is not to be comprehensive. It is, in fact, to be synthetic, to be as much a provider of a digested, abbreviated account of each of these topics." That was your answer on Wednesday, May 10th, 2006, with regard to your purpose of writing reports; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was my answer to the question of writing the Prlic report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. So the Prlic report you distinguish from all other reports that you've written?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All other reports but for the Prlic report obtain a different emphasis.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Prlic report was the only report that was not in narrative form that I have prepared for the Office of the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- before this body.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So if I take your answer as you stated, then with regard to the two reports that exist here, you went through extensive archival research; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You wrote as comprehensive a report here?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as comprehensively as I possibly could. That would be a voluminous undertaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you consider, as you review your reports, that your reports deal with the, apart from in passing, the critical issues as they relate to, for example, the Badinter Commission and the effect the Badinter Commission had upon what was occurring during late 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've treated it briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You've given it a whiff of perfume, haven't you? You haven't discussed the effect of Badinter was, did you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I belive I have in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. When you say "briefly," you mentioned Badinter, but you didn't get into the effect of what Badinter had, did you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. We'll discuss that more fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm not rising by way of objection at all, but you'll recall yesterday that Dr. Donia had his previous reports in front of him, and I have those copies that were returned to us --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm wondering if it would assist anybody if we could be provided with them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, it would assist Dr. Donia, then I'd be happy for him to have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned -- we'll get to Badinter. You mentioned that with regard to archives that -- you've been in archives primarily in Sarajevo, Belgrade, Zagreb, Budapest, Vienna, and London, for purposes of your research.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the report that you did in 2002, did you go to all of the archives that you mentioned in your direct testimony?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the report that you did in 2006, did you go to all of those archives that you mentioned in your direct testimony for purposes of - not there yet - for purposes of preparing that report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to both of these reports, during the period of time that you were preparing these reports, did you have occasion to speak with any of what I will call the "principals" who were involved in the on-the-ground activity, movement, argument, discussions, for example, Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He's a pretty important character, and I mean that in a neutral fashion, with regard to the development of what was going on during this period of time, is he not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He was alive, was he not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you attempt to speak to any of the principal players?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And who did you speak with?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I spoke extensively with Mirko Pejanovic, who was a member of the Presidency at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say "Presidency," that's the Bosnian nationalist --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the Presidency of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he was a member of the Presidency through much of the war. I've spoken to a number of party leaders from the HDZ, Stjepan Kljujic, a number of HDZ leaders, various municipal leaders. Remember, this is after the war that I'm speaking to them. But who had experienced the, let's say, life on the Serb side of the lines during the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to those individuals, are those -- did you record those sessions or take notes of those sessions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In many cases I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Did you then include those recordings and notes in the reports that you've submitted to us --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't include them, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So did you cite them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't cite to them, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I -- I don't recall that I cited to any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So we're not, at least for purposes of either a cursory or an in-depth review of your report, concerned whether or not some of the information -- the body of the information you have in your own head which forms the basis of some of the things written in your report are predicated upon conversations that you had with others or not. We can't do that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I was thinking. I forgot. Do you know who Mr. Sacirbey is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to speak with him?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There's two Sacirbeys. One is the senior, Sacirbegovic, who was around for a long time and then his son, who was the foreign minister, I believe, in the course of the war. I've spoken to them both very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, the son, he was somebody who was quite active in the negotiations through 1991/1992, was he not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe a little later in the course of things, he was very active.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And he had a definite perspective with regard to the developments in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did he not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Am I correct in my understanding that the purposes of these two reports were to offer enlightenment on the background of the major developments of events institutions that are referenced in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you said that, you're referring to the indictment that we have here in this case, and that's the indictment against Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I certainly looked -- am familiar with that indictment or looked over that indictment and saw some relevance. But the reports were prepared in response to reviewing the indictments of the particular cases involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. So with regard to -- with regard to the statement made that they were enlightenment with regard to, as I said, the major development of events and institutions referenced in the indictment, meaning the Perisic indictment, that statement is not entirely accurate, is it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you cited the statement accurately. I think my statement was that I was responding to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't want to misquote you. I don't want to misquote you. "What were the objectives, then, of these reports"? And your answer was: "I was asked by the Prosecution to prepare a report which explained in light of the background of the major developments, events, and institutions referenced in the indictment." So when you made that answer, considering what you've just said, that answer dealt with those two indictments and did not deal with the Perisic indictment, would be a proper interpretation of what you said there.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Then we're on the same page. Your reports are, as I understand it, based upon a particular theory, as you've suggested to us, an overarching theory upon which you approach this particular subject. And by that I'm referring to the language that you used, and here I want to make sure that we're talking to each other and that I'm accurate, because I don't want to be inaccurate here, which is you said, in terms of discussing the method of preparation - and I believe we start on page 1635 and go on to page 13 -- there it is. Perfect. You discussed the method of preparation, and then you say that there is a "viewpoint," at the bottom of page 1635, at line 25, "or perhaps one could call it a theory underpinning these reports." And I just want to stop there for a moment. I'll continue on with what you said. But when you say there's a "viewpoint" or a theory, I take it that that means that you were approaching these reports from a particular historical perspective, a school of thought, as it were.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A school of thought that is shared by history and several other disciplines.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that. I'm just trying to, first of all, make sure I'm understanding precisely this -- the point here, which is that your work is predicated upon a theoretical view of history that guides you through your application of the historical facts to a particular event or a particular question that's being asked of you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's kind of a long complex question. I would probably say "informed by" this approach, rather than "predicated upon."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, this is, would it be fair to say, one of a number of theories that exists with regard to historical interpretation of facts in general? That's my first question. And by that I mean nationalities and national movements are constructed entities rather than primordial ones.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't accept quite the way that you've put that question. It's more than historical. It's anthropological, political scientific, and sociological. And it's one of many theories that pertains to knowledge in general. It's one of two primary viewpoints with regard to nationalities and national movements and their origins and development.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can you parse out for us. Since you've told us that you are not an expert in sociology and you're not an expert in anthropology, can you parse out for us the extent to which your reliance as an historian is in those fields in which you're not an expert in terms of this particular theory?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as an historian, I'm always consuming information from other fields, and I've done so extensively from anthropology, which is really the, I'd say, origins of this notion. It really began as a debate between Clifford Gertz who articulated the notion that nationalities are primordial and was contested by people like Benedict Anderson who, the very title is suggestive, "Imagined Communities." And then two historians who've edited a book of essays called "The Invention of Tradition." These things overlap disciplines very easily, and the theoretical work by people like Anderson is reflected also in -- or carried out in, let's say, a more historical context by a number of authors who've applied this point of view to different parts of the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You've mentioned -- you've mentioned two authors, and perhaps now would not be a bad time to just put some more names into the mix to see whether or not these are also individuals upon which you have focused or thought about, relied on, considered. Henk Dekker?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Eric Hobsbawm?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And Homi Bhabha?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Eric Hobsbawm, he has, a matter of fact, wrote a book specifically -- or has done a lot of work specifically in the area of nations and nationalism, has he not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he has. And he was co-editor of one of the books I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. There's another fellow. I think his name is Gellner.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ernst Gellner.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Ernst Gellner. And the issue here of nationalism and national movements and nationalities is a bit, for the moment, confusing to me because I want to make sure that we're using terms that we understand, which is when you said that nationalities and national movements are constructed entities. Are you equating here nationalities and national movements as one and the same?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not equating them but stating that both are constructed entities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. So could you give us a definition for your historical purposes of what a nationality -- how you would define "nationality"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term or the meaning that I use in this context is national identity, the identity of a group which claims to be a nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in that regard, if you were to use the term, for example, "a people," a people who claim to be a nation, would that be the same term? Would we be using the same term here? Who "nationalities" equate with "people"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my usage here, yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the term "people" is the most common translation and, in my view, correct translation of the word in the B/C/S, "narod" and that has a specific meaning within political discourse in the former Yugoslavia, which refers to a people that, if you want me to define it as --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Please do because we're going to have to spend a moment or two here, if you could.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A narod, translated "people," is a nation which, and again this is in the political discourse of the region, has a homeland within the country in question. It has a republic homeland. It may have peoples in -- members of the group in other republics and even in other countries, but it is a group that is identified with a particular republic in the socialist federal republic arrangement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Does that, as you've defined it just now, go back to -- and I think this is only the time that I'm going to go back over 50 years, does that go back to the concept that was promulgated, in the Corfu Declaration I believe in 1917 or 1918, in which there was a recognition of sovereign states of peoples?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it goes more back to the Stalinist understanding of a nation and a people, in his nationality theory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When I referred to the Corfu Declaration, you know what I was referring to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At that point in time that many years ago, there was the establishment of a number of distinct states predicated upon it definition, as I understand it, and please do correct me if I'm wrong, of peoples, which were the Serbs, the Croats, and the Slovenes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among others.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Among others. And there was a recognition then of a nationality, as we're defining it, by those distinct groups.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me revise that, when you refer to the Corfu Declaration, my answer, among others, is not correct. It's wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let's make it right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers kindly not overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are being requested not to overlap. You are being requested by the interpreters not to overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So the concept of the identity of people and the concept of a sovereign state is something that has resonated within the region, and by that I'm going to talk about the former Yugoslavia, for an appreciable period of time, has it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact, over time, moving away from Stalin and into Tito, there was, in fact, a recognition of the importance of an equality between the peoples that was expressed through something that I've been told is called the key system, but I'm sure there's a specific name in B/C/S for that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the key system is kind of a different subject, but your fundamental question is quality between peoples in Tito's socialist federal scheme, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And within Tito's socialist federal scheme, there was a recognition, was there not, of distinct -- the necessity to give distinct peoples who've identified themselves as such some form of identity above and beyond the identity of being Yugoslavian. I'm sorry, I wouldn't say necessarily above and beyond the identity of being Yugoslavian. That's probably incorrect. But in addition to that of being Yugoslavian. Because he had -- he had, in fact, a real -- a real dynamic situation to work with, which were all these different peoples who identified themselves as distinct groups.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, are those peoples who identified themselves as distinct groups, are those peoples, in your terms when we're talking about the underlying theory, are they constructed entities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Rather than --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the viewpoint of -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In your viewpoint.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my viewpoint they are, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, we have -- I believe we have three major identifiable groupings, if I might.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me a time frame that you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm in 1990 through 1995.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I think three -- the three largest being Serbs, Croats, and Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to the Bosnian Muslims, the Bosnian Muslims find themselves for purposes of what we're talking about here, constructed entities, in I think somewhat of a unique position, do they not? And by that I mean that there were both ethnic as well as religious components unique to the Bosnian Muslims that held them together as a cohesive group in their mind.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's two questions there. Number 1, are they unique or somewhat unique, and my answer to that is no. Were there religious -- ethnic and religious components unique to the Bosnian Muslims? Yes, there were, just as there were to Serbs, Croats, even Jews.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, let's leave the Jews out of this one, shall we, just for the purposes of the discussion.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to -- with regard to the three groups that you've mentioned, can you define for us what you mean by "constructed entity"? Because as I'm understanding what you're saying, a constructed entity is something that occurred -- and I'm putting that in terms of rather than a primordial one, is a constructed entity is an entity that exists from the top down, whereas a primordial one is an entity that would grow from, and I can't resist in a certain sense, from the primordial views. It's something that is a natural construct over the history of time. And so I'm trying to make -- I'm trying to make sure I understand what you're saying here when you're talking about the theoretical basis upon which you're relying, which is that you have a top-down definition of a group, as opposed to something that is defined by the people to which a leader may emerge.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Could you explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With your leave, I'm just -- there's so much packed into this question, I'm not sure what part of the question "no" was an answer to, and I wonder if you could clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can you clarify what part of the no, or do you need me to break the question down? I'm happy to do it either way.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you'll give me lead to try to explain the -- I think your description of a primordial concept is pretty accurate to what their the viewpoint of those thinkers is. But on the constructed side, what constitutes a constructed entity is not necessarily top-down. It may very well be a result of inter-action between elites who were seeking to define and order a national identity or national movement and the masses who may or may not to already differentiated along the lines that the elites wishes -- whish to create. In most cases you're looking at a constructed process in which intellectuals or political leaders come along and seek to create new lines of division or differentiation between peoples. If they find no response in the populous, then the construction doesn't happen. There have been many efforts, for example, to create a Bosnian identity, going back to the 1860s. None of those have worked because they didn't respond -- there was no response from the populous.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me understand -- see if I understand you correctly here. I'm going to, for a moment, ask you to consider someone else, if you would, because this might help us all. Are you familiar with Edward Bernays?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Again, I'm not rising by way of objection at all, but I just note some of these names might be unfamiliar to my colleague, the court reporter, and for the accuracy of the record, perhaps, my friend, if you could spell sometimes for her, it will save us doing work later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We've got a deal that whenever there are any problems she comes to me, and it's taken care of. So if she doesn't know how to spell something, it's been dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You said no. I won't take that any further, except that I invite you to take a look at him. He was a nephew of Freud's and instrumental in manipulating the masses.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You're welcome. Based upon what you've said right here, if I understand you correctly, if we were to take a look at the historical view of the movements, and I'm going to give you a couple, which are the revolution in Cuba, are you suggesting that that is a movement in which the elite, and by that I mean Mr. Castro, his brother, and others, created lines of division or differentiation between people, that they found -- that they're the ones who did that and that was not a popular movement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that the case you're pointing to is one of national movement or national identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be a revolutionary movement. But I'm not, in any case, saying that this was not a popular movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The movement that we're dealing with here is not a popular movement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Again, would the speakers kindly not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And by here I'm talking about Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Again, you're being asked to please not overlap. Could you please break in between question and answer and answer and question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you ask the question again, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I can, Dr. Donia. You've said as far as you're concerned, what occurred in Cuba was not a national movement, but rather a revolutionary movement, as I understood your answer, and you were drawing a distinction between a revolutionary movement and a national movement.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I wasn't certain whether the movement in Cuba was a national movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know enough about it, really, to call it a national movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In days gone by, when we were -- when we were young and gay, there was a movement in the United States which was considered to be a national movement. That was the Civil Rights Movement. I take it that for purposes of your analysis here, that is not a national movement. And I'm asking the question just to see if I can understand.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As great as my affection is for the Civil Rights Movement, I would not classify it in terms I am using here as a national movement, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to -- if we were to take the survey of the world and we were for a moment to stop in South Africa with regard to the struggle to overcome apartheid, would that be considered to be a national movement by your definition or would that be another form of movement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to the indigenous people in Mexico who are presently in a struggle to obtain independence, once again, is that a situation that you don't know about?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say it's more likely to fall into the definition that I have for national movement, but I really don't know enough about it to so conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So part of what -- so part of what is involved in your definition of a national movement has to -- has to do with perhaps indigenous people or some kind of particular way of identifying the group; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some particular way of identifying the group. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And if we have -- and I'm going on with what your answer -- what your answer was with regard to your theory. You say: "That is a debate that has flourished in a number of disciplines over the past three decades, with the view that I share being that ethnic groups ..." So that's one area where I think we're clear about what you're defining, an ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "And national movements," and national movements, as I understand it, are defined as potentially a group of peoples who have a particular national identity.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A people that has a particular -- or seeks to define a particular national identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "Are dynamic, constantly changing phenomena that mutate over time." I understand what you're saying there. "Depending on the actions of the elites that form them and lead them."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that's the area in which I was asking you the question about being an organised movement from the top down, because as I understand the language there, as I understand this particular language, it seems to me that you're implying something in the form of a ruling intelligentsia or a ruling elite of some form that determines what is good for the people, and based upon that determination, then makes policies and decisions for the people, as opposed to listening to what the people have to say and working with their -- with what galvanises the people themselves.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you were to use the word "aspiring" instead of "dominant" or "ruling," I would, I think, accept -- agree with your statement. The makers of these movements are rarely power-holders or preordained holders of wisdom, as recognised intellectuals. They are entrepreneurs. They are aspiring intellectuals or aspiring rulers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that would be your definition then, I take it, of Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Milosevic. They were, as you put it, aspiring entrepreneurs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They certainly were in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And throughout the period of which you wrote your reports.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They ceased to -- or became less and less innovators and entrepreneurial as the period goes along.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And is that because from a historical perspective, they had obtained a certain level of power which they were holding on to, as opposed to, using your language, "aspiring towards some entrepreneurial state"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There should be. If we could have a correction on line 85, I said Karadzic and Mladic. It's written as Milosevic. I meant to say Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take it you would take the same position with Mr. Milosevic, since his name was mentioned on the transcript?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to -- and I have a better understanding of what you meant, and I hope we all have a better understanding of what you meant by that particular theory. Now, is this a theory that has been tested empirically? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen any efforts to test it in, let's say, an applied mathematics sense, if that's what you mean by "empirically."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I am talking about --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are many studies that have applied the theory through a process of assessing the historical record or the contemporary record and concluded that the theory illuminates and holds as valid for the particular subjects being discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: May I ask a question. Professor Donia, when you speak of theory, as you know, there is a very epistemological meaning of theory, which is to say a set of propositions, empirical, verifiable, and with predictability for the future. The paradigm of this law are mathematical laws. Rather than theory, in this context of social sciences which could not equate the theorys of social sciences, what you call viewpoint or theory would be rather a theoretical orientation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I fully agree. That is a better description of it than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: So the usage of "theory" does not correspond in your usage to either strict theorys in the political sciences, but rather what will be called empirical generalisations apart from theory and are just viewpoints, workable hypotheses of explanation. So what you call theory is rather an instrumental or realistic way of an hypothesis to be applied to a given mass of data.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I absolutely agree, and you put it certainly much better than I ever could or would. But I think the -- one of the points that you're making is its explanatory power is the test, in a sense, in lieu of the strict empirical kind of result that one would have in such a theoretical --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: You use also the term, and I hope you will discount my intervention from the time allotted to the Defence, you have used also "empirical narrative ." In one of the phrases in the last session, you said in page 17, lines 3 to 4, "empirically based narrative accounts, topically organised of the major developments and institutions pertaining to these topics," and then you refer, as the Defence said, about the indictment. To what extent is theoretical broad orientation which is that vessel like this. I have been familiar for the last four years with all the theories in relation from anthropologists, from Radcliffe, Rowan and Malinovski to Robert Redfield and whatever, you know. I have tragically enough taught sociology for 20 years at an US university. To what extent your report will have been oriented in different way had you accepted the primordial structure of the theory? And give me concrete examples, given the fact that you're saying here it's an empirically based narrative account. It's not a theory. It's not a prediction. It's not amenable to verification because of the large mass amount of data. And I don't know of any theory in history or sociology who has been able to empirically be verified. And I'm talking of all the literature of sociology in the last 50 years up to this point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. How would it be different if it were informed by the primordial view? I think it would be much more related to the distant past as a factor that molded behaviour in the period in question, starting with 1990. By "distant," I mean as far back as the Middle Ages, as recently, perhaps, as the Second World War, and viewed those developments as sort of baked into the identity of the primordial entity that we are examining. So it would have a much longer, let's say, horizon and argue for direct causation from events in the relatively distant past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Do you believe that your conclusions in the report given the constraints of the past outlined by the Prosecutor? Because you said, "I was asked by the Prosecutor --" on page 16, lines 24: "I was asked by the Prosecutor to write a report which explained and enlightened the background of the major institutions and referred to in the indictment," which the Defence has just cited. In what ways -- or in which ways the conclusions of your report will have been different from the present ones in relating decisions, in analysing the data?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a very good question. I'm kind of hard-wired to think the other way, and so it's difficult maybe for me to think through that. But I would say, at least preliminary, without giving it a bigger think, is that I would trace the origins of the major institutions to much earlier time periods and the proclivities or the behaviour of the actors to reprising those of historical personalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You've given us four separate criteria that you applied in your analysis of the documents that you used as being important in determining how to choose, what to choose, why to choose. Those were relevance, reliability, verifiability, and richness; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
