utterances.text: With regard to the issue of relevance, you chose, based upon the information that was given to you by the Prosecution and the particular question that they asked you to proceed upon, which was pertaining to that which was referenced in two indictments, the Krajisnik indictment and the Dragomir Milosevic indictment, that information that you felt applied directly to those two indictments; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's a long convoluted question. I can parse it, if you wish. I would say that the information was referenced or the issues set forth in the indictment. I don't know I would accept the formulation that it was applied directly. The materials that I used were only in small matter those that were given to me by the Prosecution, and the import of your question suggests that I based it on the information given to me by the Prosecution. I certainly was seeking to respond to the particular question that was asked of me but not solely or even principally upon the information that was given to me by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What was the specific question that was asked of you by Mr. Tieger with regard to your report concerning the Krajisnik indictment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What was the specific question asked of you -- was it someone other than Mr. Tieger, that asked you to become involved in the Dragomir Milosevic report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe it was Susan Somers, but I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Assuming that you're correct, and we can identify a Prosecutor, assuming it was Ms. Somers, be that as it may, once again, what was the specific question, what was the specific task, that you were asked to perform as regards the Dragomir Milosevic indictment, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the specific question. The task that I was asked to perform, I indicated, I believe, yesterday, it was to address those issues, institutions, and developments suggested or referenced in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And did you -- was -- after you received the original request, were you involved in any kind of colloquies back and forth, or just after receiving the original request, for example, from Mr. Tieger, did you go off and write the report, submit it to him, without any further conversation? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did submit a draft for the Prosecutors to review.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before you submitted the draft, did you have any conversation with the Prosecution concerning the direction in which the report was going, concerning questions that had arisen in your mind as you were writing the draft report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Once you submitted the draft for review, did you have any memorialised, once again, communications with the Prosecution concerning the draft that you had prepared and submitted for their review?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After you submitted the draft for their review, did you have occasion to modify, edit, the report in any manner?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly to edit, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take it the same would be true, so we don't have to go through all the same questions, I take it the same would be true with regard to the report that you submitted in the Dragomir Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've indicated that another important factor for you is that of reliability.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if I'm not mistaken, reliability was defined in two different ways. How you determined a document's reliability, you defined it in two different ways. That's what you told us yesterday. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the two different ways that I defined it. Please could I --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. The question was asked: How do you determine reliability? How do you make an assessment of the document's reliability? And your answer, this is on page 1367: "There are two ways one can do that. First you look at the source. The words of an actor in a particular event clearly bear more weight and have greater validity than there was of a third- or fourth-hand person or someone who is not in a position to directly observe events." So in that situation, when, for example, you are reviewing the stenographic notes of an SDS session, you are in a situation where you are hearing -- hearing or reading verbatim what the individual said.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the document's reliability, there are two issues, then, that flow from that, which is, 1, is the document itself is an accurate account of what transpired. That's one kind of reliability, correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the other is is whether or not the words that are being spoken are, in fact, internally true words.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in that regard you have to take a look at a series of other issues. You have to take a look at, for example, what was the purpose of those words in any given context. Were they political in nature? Were they directive in nature? Were they in response to a particular situation or were they in response to an argument that was had on the floor? I mean, there are a myriad of different things you have to make a determination about with regard to the issue of reliability, meaning that the words spoken actually mean, have a particular meaning; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you say that the second -- then you go on to say: "So that character of the source is the first important thing," and I think we understand what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You're not talking about the character of the individual, whether somebody has a good character or a bad character, for example, in your estimation.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nature of the source.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Nature of the source. The second thing would be from the outside, the value of the document from other documents that were generated at the time. And if I understand, what you mean by that, what you're saying is that if I'm looking at one particular document, I'm going to engage in a comparative analysis with other documents to see whether or not I'm picking up the same information, contradictory information, how the document -- how the document responds to the issues that are addressed within itself as an internal matter.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the sources -- in terms of the sources that you used in your report, you've used a variety of different sources.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Some of those sources, for example, are what I would call, just for the moment, primary verbatim sources, like the one we were just talking about where you have the actual words of a speaker.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And there can be little dispute over whether there's any interpretation with regard to those -- to the actual words that are spoken. The meaning may be different, but the actual words can be little dispute about.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There will inevitably be disputes about them, but in general it is the highest level of reliability.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. You also -- you also have documents which are documents that you received that were interpreted documents, and by that, where the spoken word in B/C/S was translated into the English word, written. Am I correct in that regard?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very rarely in this case was -- or in my long investigations and in preparing specifically for these papers was that the case. Very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to those, those sources that you relied upon where you were listening to the -- did you have any audio?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never listened to any more than a few audiotapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So you did not have to worry about the age-old adage "Tradutiore e traditore"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Translation is trigger; right? Trigger. With regard to another source that you used, another source that you used were newspaper articles.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And another source that you used were books.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And papers.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to the books and papers, what you did then is you read the views of others who you either deemed to be experts in the field or deemed to have some knowledge in the field or had even written about in the field and drew your own conclusions from that information. So you were interpreting their interpretation -- you were doing two things. You were interpreting their interpretation of facts, and you were gleaning from them those facts that they presented.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all books are scholarly accounts. Some of those books are memoirs and personal recollections. So I think the answer to your question is partially, yes, I'm involved in a process of reading and assessing secondary accounts, accounts by scholars, but a lot of that information that comes into my world of preparation is, in fact, the written words of participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you mentioned there memoirs and personal recollections. Now, with regard to the issue of -- with regard to the issue of reliability and accuracy, I'm now paraphrasing here, and I'm wondering whether or not you take this on -- you took this on when you were doing that, I believe it may have been Mr. Churchill who said, "History will be kind to me, since I'm writing my own memoirs."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is typical of memoirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right, which is that the individual casts themselves in a particular position. So when you're dealing with memoirs, that is ann area which you take with a grain, and I'm asking you here, you take with a grain of salt.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't say a grain of salt. I think it has to be critically assessed in the sense of "critically" that we referred to yesterday, an objective assessment of the account is more likely to be objective or accurate if, in fact, the writer does put him or herself into an unfavourable light at times.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And in that same regard, when you're dealing with memoirs, do you take into account, for example, something else that was said, which is that anyone who believes you can't change history has never tried to write his memoirs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I missed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. Anyone who believes you can't change history has never tried to write his memoirs. That would been expression, a pretty clear expression of the power of the pen to change the facts that actually occurred, would it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: For your purposes, that was said by Mr. Ben Gurion. Now, with regard to the issue of richness, one of the things I've noted in your report, and refreshingly so, is that you use not only language but you use a tone of presentation which is, let me put it this way, convincing to the reader, and I commend you for that, and I'm very serious when I say that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as I understood, since your craft is that of writing history, one of the things you've attempted to do both in your writing away from these reports as well as in terms of the writing of these reports is you've attempted to present the information in a way that is not only palatable, but it is also convincing.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a major aim, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And in terms of being convincing, it's convincing with regard to -- with regard to the conclusions that you've drawn. I mean, you just don't throw out a bunch of facts and say, Here's a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. And the narrative itself is partly persuasive in character, in that I'm attempting to persuade the reader that I have correctly connected the facts referenced in the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In that regard, and perhaps we'll speak about this probably not in the time that we have left today, probably tomorrow, but in that regard, for example, what you've done in a number of places in your report is you've quoted somebody and then you have a bridging sentence and then there's another quote, and in leading that whole phrase, one comes away with a particular viewpoint based upon the bridging sentence. Do you understand what I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mm-hm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That, as a matter of fact, is a function of what you did as a writer in order to convince the reader of the position you take. You take a fact, you then put in your opinion or interpretation, and you put in another fact. There's nothing wrong with that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite that simple, but I agree, in essence, that that's the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I want to return just for a moment to the issue of the newspaper that you used. As I recall, you relied on a newspaper, and I'm sure I'm going to mispronounce it, so I apologise to everybody, you relied on a newspaper that was called Oslobodjenje.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very good, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And you also relied on NIN and Glas.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But Oslobodjenje obtained a kind of a different position than NIN and Glas, if I'm not mistaken, because I believe you define that one as being a newspaper of record. Am I correct? Or were all three of them newspapers of record?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe NIN was. But Glas and Oslobodjenje were newspapers of records -- of record, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And a newspaper of record is something that has, and I'm asking whether you would agree with this, high standards of journalism? One component.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To distinguish between its function as a newspaper of record and its editorial approach, newspaper of record will try to maintain very close position to the actual sources of information --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and to provide essential data, it may have an editorial approach which may tend to discount the information that it conveys or argue with it. But the essential function of the -- a function of the newspaper of record is, indeed, to do that reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In that regard, would you agree that the articles that are presented in a newspaper of record such as Oslobodjenje, which was a newspaper of record, as I understand it, in your estimation.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It served that function, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Established a definitive record of current events; is that --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do we like that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And would you also agree with me that such a newspaper would have a policy, both in its editorial aspect and its news-gathering functions, which would be considered to be professional and unbiased?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So for purposes of our discussion, the issues -- I take it your "no" was probably more focused on the "unbiased" than it was on the "professional."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me a question about its editorial aspect and its news-gathering functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer to the news-gathering functions is it seeks to be objective and unbiased, but I don't -- I don't think there's a newspaper that has an editorial policy that is deliberately neutral or even unbiased.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to the one newspaper that you have identified as a newspaper of record, that being Oslobodjenje, I take it that you take the position that with regard to its news-gathering function, the manner in which it gathered news, it was, in your estimation, unbiased?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me correct you and say I also identified Glas --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- as a newspaper of record.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But just with regard to Oslobodjenje first. Glas is another matter.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite. I think the news-gathering function includes being a newspaper of record but also includes gathering news through investigative journalism, reports of commentators. So I would say the news -- the paper-of-record function is only part of its news-gathering philosophy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What I'm driving at, and I appreciate that expansion of your answer, what I'm driving at, and this is my last question, and I was hoping to be able to go quite at it now, is that in your estimation, they were unbiased. There was no bias in the gathering of the news.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, okay. Then we will pick up tomorrow what your position is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll then stand adjourned to tomorrow morning, 9.00, Courtroom I. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 20th day of November, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
